answer.label: Not Emma Goldman — actually Margaret C. Anderson
answer.authorDates: 1886–1973 · founder, editor and publisher of The Little Review
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is a description of Emma Goldman, not a sentence by her. It first turns up as an unsigned footnote — keyed [1] to the poem “White Mists,” signed “M. C. A.” — on page 16 of The Little Review, May 1916 ↗ — the magazine Margaret C. Anderson founded, edited and copyrighted — introducing Goldman’s own “Letters from Prison”: “In the year of our Lord 1916 Emma Goldman was sent to jail for advocating that ‘women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open.’” Goldman’s biographer Alix Kates Shulman quotes it as Anderson’s observation ↗, and the line appears nowhere in Goldman’s own published writing.

source.excerpt: In the year of our Lord 1916 Emma Goldman was sent to jail for advocating that “women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open.” Some extracts from letters written during her fifteen-day sentence appear on the next page.
trail: The earliest printing we could locate is an unsigned footnote, keyed [1] to Anderson’s own signed poem “White Mists,” on page 16 of The Little Review, May 1916 (Vol. 3, No. 3) ↗, introducing Emma Goldman’s “Letters from Prison,” written during a fifteen-day sentence in the Queen’s County Jail.
The magazine was founded, edited and published by Margaret C. Anderson ↗, whose name carries the 1916 copyright line on the issue; the bound volume can be read in facsimile at the Internet Archive ↗.

Goldman’s biographer Alix Kates Shulman quotes the sentence as Anderson’s — “Margaret Anderson of The Little Review observed” — in the biographical essay she wrote for Emma Goldman, The Traffic in Women and Other Essays on Feminism (Times Change Press, 1970) ↗.

A word-search of the complete 1906–1917 run of Goldman’s own magazine Mother Earth ↗, together with Anarchism and Other Essays, The Social Significance of the Modern Drama and My Disillusionment in Russia, returns no instance of the sentence — and Wikiquote’s Goldman page ↗ does not list it at all.
source.excerptNote: The note is set in italics at the foot of the page, printed as footnote [1] and keyed to the title of the poem “White Mists,” which is signed “M. C. A.” It sits immediately above Goldman’s letters, which are datelined “Queen’s County Jail, Long Island City, New York. April, 1916.” The famous sentence sits inside a subordinate clause describing what Goldman was jailed for — it is not printed as a quotation from any Goldman speech or essay.

Later reprintings that quote the line, such as the 1970 Times Change Press pamphlet, hold copyright only in their own new text.

author.name: Margaret C. Anderson
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1886–1973 · American editor, founder of The Little Review
author.bio: Margaret Caroline Anderson founded The Little Review in Chicago in 1914 and ran it as editor and publisher until 1929, printing Sherwood Anderson, Amy Lowell, Ben Hecht, Ezra Pound — and Emma Goldman, whom she had championed since first hearing her lecture. Jane Heap joined as co-editor in 1916. Anderson is best remembered for serialising James Joyce’s Ulysses, a decision that got the magazine prosecuted for obscenity; the sentence about mouths and wombs was a throwaway editorial note she wrote to introduce Goldman’s prison letters.

misattribution.heading: How Goldman came to own a line about her
misattribution.intro: This is the rare misattribution where the credited person is genuinely the subject of the sentence — just not its author. Anderson wrote a one-line gloss on why Goldman went to jail; a half-century later the gloss was reprinted, printed onto protest posters that circulated widely, and finally uploaded to quote sites as though Goldman had said it herself.

items.why: The line is embedded in a subordinate clause about Goldman in her editor’s note — “sent to jail for advocating that …” — and it does not appear in her books or anywhere in Mother Earth ↗, the magazine she edited from 1906 to 1917.

Moderna Museet records that the anarcho-feminist artist Monica Sjöö “would often cite Goldman’s words” — this line among them — on posters that were widely spread ↗ in campaigns for abortion rights and sexual freedom.

Anderson founded, edited and published The Little Review, and the 1916 issue carries her copyright; Alix Kates Shulman names her as the source of the observation in her 1970 biographical essay on Goldman ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Goldman went to jail for the argument; Anderson wrote the sentence. The wording belongs to The Little Review of May 1916 ↗, not to Emma Goldman.

context.heading: An editor’s one-line verdict
lead: Goldman was in the Queen’s County Jail in Long Island City in April 1916, serving fifteen days for publicly explaining contraception. She sent out letters, and The Little Review printed extracts from them in its May issue. To set them up, the editor wrote forty-odd words at the foot of the previous page — and one clause of that note turned out to be the most quotable thing anyone would ever write about her.

Margaret C. Anderson was an open Goldman partisan running an avant-garde magazine out of Chicago’s Fine Arts Building, one that would later be prosecuted for serialising Ulysses. The compression — mouths shut, wombs open — is the work of a professional editor summarising a case, which is exactly why it travels better than the paragraphs Goldman actually wrote.
detailsBody: The note carries no byline, which is normal for editorial matter in a magazine that small; Anderson was founder, editor, publisher and copyright holder, and the note is keyed as footnote [1] to the title of the poem printed directly above it, which is signed with her initials, “M. C. A.” Alix Kates Shulman, writing in 1970, attributes the remark to “Margaret Anderson of The Little Review” without qualification.

One honest caveat: the note does put the phrase inside quotation marks, so it is possible Anderson was condensing a formulation Goldman used from the platform rather than coining it herself. Nothing in Goldman’s printed work — her books, her essays, or eleven years of Mother Earth — contains it, so on the available evidence the wording is Anderson’s.
context.pull: Goldman went to jail for the argument. Her editor wrote the sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Little Review, May 1916 (Vol. 3, No. 3), edited by Margaret C. Anderson, contains the editorial note: "In the year of our Lord 1916 Emma Goldman was sent to jail for advocating that 'women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open.' Some extracts from letters written during her fifteen-day sentence appear on the next page." — printed immediately before Emma Goldman's "Letters from Prison," datelined Queen's County Jail, Long Island City, New York, April 1916.

The scanned bound volume of The Little Review vol. 3 shows the same note on page 16, with the issue masthead 'VOL. III MAY, 1916 NO. 3', 'MARGARET C. ANDERSON, EDITOR', and 'Copyright, 1916, by Margaret C. Anderson'; the contents page lists 'White Mists — M. C. A.' and 'Letters from Prison — Emma Goldman'.

Emma Goldman, The Traffic in Women and Other Essays on Feminism (Times Change Press, copyright 1970), with a biography by Alix Kates Shulman, states: 'Margaret Anderson of The Little Review observed, "Emma Goldman was sent to prison for advocating that women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open."' Its credits page notes Shulman's essay previously appeared in Women: A Journal of Liberation, Spring 1970.
The complete Mother Earth run (1906–1917), Emma Goldman's own magazine, contains no instance of the phrase 'wombs open' or 'mouths shut and their wombs open' across its machine-readable issues.

Wikiquote's Emma Goldman page does not list 'Women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open' in any section; its Disputed section covers only the 'If voting changed anything' quotation.

Moderna Museet states that Monica Sjöö 'would often cite Goldman's words: "Women need not always keep their mouths shut and their wombs open" and "Women are the real left", on posters that were widely spread' in protests and campaigns for abortion rights and sexual freedom.
Margaret Caroline Anderson (November 24, 1886 – October 19, 1973) was the American founder, editor and publisher of the art and literary magazine The Little Review.
The Little Review was an American avant-garde literary magazine founded by Margaret Anderson in Chicago's Fine Arts Building, published from 1914 to May 1929; Jane Heap became co-editor in 1916.
